**Subject:** Extended-duration flight recorders (25 h CVR / 140+ h FDR, low-SWaP design) | **Evidence base:** Tier 2 public sources only — no user/CRM data supplied | **Date window:** 2021–Sep 2026 (pre-2021 used only for long-term trend)

## Governing Insight

**Situation.** Crash-protected flight recorders are a non-discretionary, regulation-triggered equipment category supplied by a small group of certified specialists, and a US/EASA mandate cycle has now converted 25-hour cockpit voice recording from a differentiator into a baseline specification (FACT, High — Future Market Insights, May 2026; AVweb, 2 Feb 2026).

**Complication.** Two structural events landed inside eighteen months: the recorder business changed hands (L3Harris Commercial Aviation Solutions → Acron Aviation, closed 31 March 2025) and its principal rival's parent split apart (Honeywell Aerospace spun off 29 June 2026) — while Airbus simultaneously selected a single qualified 25-hour CVR and moved supply into its own service-bulletin channel (FACT, High).

**Question.** Where does competitive advantage actually sit in a market where the headline performance claim (25 h audio / 140+ h data) is now met by multiple vendors?

**Answer.** Advantage has migrated away from recording duration and toward *channel control and installation economics*. The 140-hour data figure is already exceeded by a competitor (Curtiss-Wright publishes 210+ h at 4,096 wps), and weight parity between the two leading commercial units is within ~0.3 lb (SRVIVR25 9.79 lb vs HCR-25 <9.5 lb) — so the single most consequential 2025 development is not a product spec but Acron's Airbus qualification and service-bulletin route to market, which converts a hardware sale into an OEM-mediated one. *So what:* on public evidence, the competitive contest in this segment is being decided at the airframer/STC layer, not the datasheet layer.

## Market size: the published range is not usable as-is

**FACT (Medium).** Published estimates for this market span roughly 30× — from USD 87.3 M (Credence, Jun 2025) and USD 117.9 M (Mordor, 2025) to USD 1.88 B (360iResearch, ~Aug 2026) and USD 4.70 B (Market Research Future, Apr 2026). **OBSERVATION (Medium):** the lower cluster (~USD 90–225 M) appears to measure crash-protected recorder *hardware*; the multi-billion cluster appears to bundle recording systems, data acquisition units, services and flight-data analytics. No source publishes a reconciliation. *So what:* any revenue plan anchored to the multi-billion figures is sizing a different market than the one in which SRVIVR25 and HCR-25 compete.

**Internal bottom-up estimate (Medium confidence).** Peak-year global 25 h-CVR-class hardware demand ≈ **USD 120 M/yr**, composed of:

- US retrofit cohort: 13,500 aircraft (NTSB, via Forbes, 14 Feb 2024 — aircraft required to carry both CVR and FDR) × USD 25,000 per CVR (FAA NPRM costing input, *an analytical assumption, not an observed market price*) = USD 337.5 M, spread across the 2026–2030 compliance window (statutory 2030 retrofit deadline; AVweb/NBAA) ≈ **USD 67.5 M/yr**.
- Global line-fit: 44,000 deliveries / 20 years (Boeing CMO, 18 Jul 2026) = ~2,200 aircraft/yr × 1 CVR per aircraft (**assumption**) × USD 25,000 = **USD 55 M/yr**.

Explicitly excluded: FDR units, RIPS, installation labour, military recorders, and non-US retrofit (EASA's 25 h requirement predates the US rule, so much of that demand is already absorbed). **Reconciliation:** the estimate falls *inside* the lower external cluster and roughly 15–35× *below* the upper cluster — consistent with the interpretation that the two clusters measure different scopes.

**Sensitivity note (FACT, High):** the FAA's own final-rule framing uses an *incremental* cost of ~USD 5,209 per aircraft in 2024 dollars, not USD 25,000. On that basis the US retrofit cohort represents only ~USD 70 M in total. That figure measures the *cost delta of compliance*, not the value of hardware shipped — which is why the full-unit basis is used above. *So what:* the choice of cost basis alone moves the retrofit market by ~5×.

## Competitive activity

**OBSERVATION (High).** Three of the eight named competitors are not verifiable participants in the 25 h CVR class on public evidence: Thales lists no crash-protected recorder in its own catalogue (its verified tie is the ACSS JV with Acron); RUAG International disclosed completion of its exit from non-space businesses in March 2026, contradicting a February 2026 analyst listing naming it a CVFDR supplier; and Leonardo DRS shows no 2024–2026 recorder announcement, appearing instead as Acron's deployable-unit partner. **Also a material correction:** Universal Avionics is an *Elbit Systems* company, not a Safran company. *So what:* the credible head-to-head set in this class is narrower than the eight-name framing implies — Acron, Honeywell (supplied by Curtiss-Wright), Curtiss-Wright, and Universal Avionics.

**FACT (High).** Honeywell's HCR-25 is built on Curtiss-Wright Fortress technology under a 2019 partnership in which Curtiss-Wright is the exclusive supplier. *So what:* two of the four apparent competitors share one manufacturing base in Bournemouth, England, reducing effective supplier diversity below the vendor count.

**FACT (High).** Safran's crash-protected helicopter CVFDR records 25 h of *data* and 2 h of audio — placing it outside the 25 h-voice comparison set. **INTERPRETATION (Medium):** Safran's relevance here is rotorcraft/defence-adjacent, not commercial 25 h CVR.

**UNKNOWN.** Vendor unit shipments, market shares, list prices and warranty terms — none published by any named firm.

## Customer demand changes

- **FACT (High).** Air transport demand is bifurcated: mandatory retrofit for Part 121 / 30+ seat aircraft by 2030, versus line-fit-only obligation for business aviation (post-16 May 2025 manufacture, ≥27,000 kg, ≤29 seats). NBAA's Doug Carr publicly welcomed the absence of a bizav retrofit mandate. *So what:* bizav 25 h demand is discretionary and modernisation-driven, not compliance-forced.
- **FACT (High), attributed.** Universal Avionics CEO Dror Yahav describes "a remarkable retrofit market opportunity"; Acron cites overnight ARINC 757 upgrades. **Tension (FACT, High):** the FAA RIA states 25 h units swap for 2 h units "without much difficulty," while the FAA also reported industry estimates that retrofit costs run ~6× line-fit. *So what:* installation friction is contested in the public record, and it is the variable that determines whether the 2030 wave is a smooth aftermarket flow or a shop-slot bottleneck.
- **FORECAST (Medium).** Asia-Pacific is projected the fastest-growing region (Mordor, Spherical), India at 7.4% CAGR (FMI, May 2026).

## Macroeconomic and external forces

**FACT (High).** Curtiss-Wright's FY2025 risk disclosures explicitly name new tariffs and retaliatory measures — a stated exposure, not a quantified impact. **FACT (High).** Curtiss-Wright reported FY2025 orders of USD 4.1 B, +10%, book-to-bill 1.2×, backlog +18% — company-wide, not recorder-specific. **FACT (High).** Boeing's 2026 CMO forecasts ~44,000 deliveries over 20 years and a fleet approaching 50,000 by 2045. *So what:* the demand floor for this category is set by build rates and fleet size, both currently expanding, which makes production cadence — not mandate timing — the durable volume driver after 2030.

## Industry shifts

**OBSERVATION (High).** Form-fit-function replacement is the universal design constraint (Acron: same dimensions/mounting points; Curtiss-Wright: form-and-fit; Universal: adapter tray). **OBSERVATION (Medium).** Differentiation is migrating to standards headroom (ED-112A → ED-112B), connectivity (HCR-25 + Aspire SATCOM streaming for GADSS), spares standardisation, and adjacent services (Universal's readout services, May 2024; third-party download tooling supporting seven-plus recorder brands). **OBSERVATION (Medium).** Adjacent white space is forming in AAM/UAS lightweight recorders (Acron xLDR) and MRO vertical entry (Lufthansa Technik markets its own 25 h-capable CVFDR). *So what:* the value pool is broadening from box sales toward channel position, data services and installed-base servicing.

**Data caution (FACT, Medium).** Acron's own materials state both "more than 25 hours" and "50+ hours" of voice recording for SRVIVR25. *So what:* the subject product's headline spec is internally inconsistent in public marketing and cannot be treated as a single verified number.

## Confidence Summary

The structural spine of this report rests on **High-confidence** evidence: the Acron–Airbus selection, the FAA final rule and its revised cost figures, the L3Harris divestiture and Honeywell separation, Curtiss-Wright's SEC-filed recorder commentary, and the RUAG exit are all sourced to company releases, government publications or wire/trade reporting with named attribution. **Medium confidence** covers vendor-published SWaP specs (single-source, self-reported), all market-size figures, the internal bottom-up estimate, and the Thales/Leonardo DRS negative findings — which are absences of public evidence rather than proof of absence. **Low confidence** applies to the multi-billion-dollar market estimates and to analyst vendor listings that company disclosures contradict.

Principal knowledge gaps: (1) no pricing, warranty or unit-volume data for any vendor — all cost figures are FAA analytical assumptions; (2) no per-vendor market share; (3) Thales and RUAG recorder participation unresolved; (4) Leonardo DRS ADFR programme status undisclosed since a lapsed 2021 EIS target; (5) no reconciliation of the 29,651 vs 29,561 fleet-count discrepancy; (6) no carbon or lifecycle sustainability claims found from any vendor. Tier 1 user data (win/loss, RFQ, distributor feedback) would close gaps 1, 2 and 6 fastest.
